title: The Fencing Of The Commons
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) explain enclosure of the English commons, from medieval open-field strip farming and the Statute of Merton (c. 1235), through the Black Death and the rise of sheep grazing, to the parliamentary enclosure acts (about 4,000 acts, 1750 to 1860) and the Industrial Revolution. They cover the Norfolk four-course system and Jethro Tull's seed drill, the Black Act and hangings of poachers, the fens drainage fight, resistance such as the Diggers and Levellers, the Highland Clearances, Russia's serf emancipation, and the 1876 Commons Act and National Trust hedge protection. The episode closes with a listener email about the origins of Easter and the pagan roots of the days of the week.

segments.title: Opening banter and definition
segments.summary: The hosts joke around, then introduce fencing the commons as the process of separating commoners from land they had used, and refer listeners to the Tragedy of the Commons episode.

segments.title: Medieval open fields and commons
segments.summary: Normans after 1066 divided England into manors with peasant villages and commons. Commoners held use rights to strip-farmed open fields, rotated crops across fields with shared animals and oxen, and used the waste (forest, rivers) for hunting, fishing and gathering.

segments.title: Life and inequality in the peasant village
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the commons system was communal, its hardships, uneven land distribution, an income cap, and the elected local council that allocated strips.

segments.title: Statute of Merton and the Black Death
segments.summary: The Statute of Merton (around 1235) allowed lords to enclose part of their land if enough common land remained. The Black Death killed about half of England's population, creating labor shortages and shifting the economy toward sheep grazing.

segments.title: First wave of enclosure and sheep
segments.summary: Wool prices made sheep profitable, so lords enclosed land with hedges and fences and displaced villages, sometimes by force. Thomas More's Utopia criticized the sheep, and Henry VII slowed enclosures.

segments.title: Second wave: parliamentary enclosure and agricultural revolution
segments.summary: A later, more intense wave tied to textiles and the Industrial Revolution. The Norfolk four-course system (wheat, turnips, barley, clover) was promoted by Lord Townshend, and the seed drill was introduced by Jethro Tull.

segments.title: Parliamentary enclosure acts
segments.summary: Enclosure was done through acts of Parliament requiring supermajority local consent, which was easy because the enclosers were in Parliament or were friends with local approvers. About 4,000 acts passed between 1750 and 1860, enclosing roughly a fifth of England, including the waste.

segments.title: Resistance, the Black Act and poaching
segments.summary: Resistance included violence against fences, the Peasants Revolt of 1381, the Diggers of the English Civil War, and commoners called the Blacks who poached deer and destroyed trees. The Black Act made poaching a capital crime and hundreds were hanged.

segments.title: The fens and Arthur Young
segments.summary: Draining the fens for crops was contested by fen peasants, who lost out in the 1700s. Arthur Young, a pro-enclosure official, later wrote a critical report in 1801 that the board rejected. Around 350 villages vanished.

segments.title: Chartists, cultural response and urban migration
segments.summary: The Chartists pushed for workers' and agrarian rights and tried to buy enclosed land back, but went bankrupt. Poets and writers reacted, and enclosure drove people into cities where vagrancy was a crime.

segments.title: Consequences: wealth, poverty and population
segments.summary: Enclosure fed the Industrial Revolution and British Empire; the enclosed wastes supplied Navy timber. Discussion of wages, malnutrition and relief, and Thomas Malthus's population essay.

segments.title: Population growth, Russia and Scotland
segments.summary: Population roughly doubled in the century after 1750 and agriculture grew more efficient. Russia's 1861 serf emancipation led to similar land loss and contributed to the Russian Revolution. Britain exported enclosure to its colonies, and the Scottish Highland Clearances displaced Highlanders.

segments.title: Surviving commons, Commons Act and National Trust
segments.summary: Some commons survive, such as Laxton's open fields and the Oxford Freemen's meadow. Enclosure ended after the Commons Preservation Society pushed the 1876 Commons Act; the National Trust now protects hedges.

segments.title: Listener mail: Easter and paganism
segments.summary: A listener named Christina writes about Judaism's influence on Easter, noting Pascua and Passover. The hosts also discuss the pagan roots of the days of the week.
